question: What blood pressure reading classifies a patient as having Stage 1 hypertension?

options.B: Systolic at least 140 mmHg or diastolic at least 90 mmHg
options.C: Systolic below 120 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg
options.D: Systolic 120-129 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg

explanation: Stage 1 hypertension starts when systolic blood pressure reaches 130 to 139 mmHg or diastolic reaches 80 to 89 mmHg. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why is a single high blood pressure reading insufficient to diagnose chronic hypertension?

options.A: Standard cuffs only work properly after three successive inflations
options.B: Blood pressure naturally stays identical throughout every hour of the day
options.C: Digital sphygmomanometers are generally inaccurate during the first measurement
options.D: Transient stress, pain, or activity can temporarily elevate blood pressure readings

explanation: Temporary factors like anxiety or physical exertion can spike readings, requiring repeated assessments to confirm true hypertension. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h1)

question: Secondary hypertension is most commonly caused by which underlying medical condition?
explanation: Kidney disease is the leading identifiable secondary cause of high blood pressure due to fluid regulation failure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h2)

question: How does excessive dietary sodium contribute to the development of hypertension?

options.A: It causes water retention, increasing total blood volume and vascular pressure
options.B: It paralyzes the baroreceptors located in the carotid sinus permanently
options.C: It decreases cardiac output by blocking electrical impulses in the myocardium
options.D: It directly dissolves the endothelial lining inside large peripheral arteries

explanation: High sodium pulls water into the bloodstream, raising the volume of fluid pressing against arterial walls. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is hypertension frequently referred to in clinical practice as the silent killer?

options.A: It only affects patients who fail to report their headaches to nurses
options.B: It completely avoids detection on all standard mercury sphygmomanometers
options.C: It results in sudden cardiac arrest without warning signs during sleep
options.D: It causes severe internal damage long before any outward symptoms appear

explanation: The lack of early symptoms allows the disease to damage organs quietly until a major event occurs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h3)

question: A patient with long-standing hypertension reports a dull morning headache and dizziness. What does this indicate?

options.A: A completely normal physiological adjustment to morning routines
options.B: Complete normalization of systemic vascular resistance
options.C: A minor allergic reaction to routine dietary salt consumption
options.D: Significant blood pressure elevation affecting cerebral circulation

explanation: Headaches and dizziness in hypertensive patients often signal poorly controlled or severely elevated blood pressure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is the result of using a blood pressure cuff that is too small for a patient's arm?

options.B: Instant rupture of the brachial artery

explanation: A cuff that is too small requires excessive pressure to compress the artery, resulting in falsely elevated readings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h4)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic running and immediately sits down for a blood pressure check. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Record the immediate high reading as proof of stage 2 hypertension
options.B: Administer a sublingual antihypertensive drug to lower the spike
options.C: Send the patient home immediately without taking any measurements
options.D: Allow the patient to rest quietly for five minutes before measuring

explanation: Physical activity spikes readings temporarily, so resting allows the cardiovascular system to return to a true baseline. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which dietary pattern is specifically recommended to help lower blood pressure naturally?

options.A: High protein ketogenic meal replacement plan
options.C: Strictly liquid low calorie fasting routine

explanation: The DASH diet focuses on nutrient-rich foods that naturally help reduce systemic blood pressure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h5)

question: Why is regular aerobic exercise encouraged as part of hypertension management?

options.A: It improves overall cardiovascular conditioning and reduces peripheral vascular resistance
options.B: It forces the kidneys to excrete all remaining potassium in the blood
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any future medical screenings
options.D: It stops the heart from beating faster during periods of emotional stress

explanation: Aerobic activity strengthens the heart and keeps blood vessels flexible, lowering overall resistance to blood flow. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h5)

question: What is a major risk if a patient stops taking their antihypertensive medication abruptly?
explanation: Stopping blood pressure drugs suddenly can cause a dangerous spike in pressure known as rebound hypertension. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h6)

question: A patient starting a new antihypertensive medication reports feeling dizzy when standing up quickly. What nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Advise the patient to double the next dose of the medication
options.B: Report an emergency cardiac arrest to the medical team immediately
options.C: Teach the patient to change positions slowly from sitting to standing
options.D: Instruct the patient to stop all fluid intake for the rest of the day

explanation: Dizziness upon standing indicates orthostatic hypotension, which can be managed by postural adjustments. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h6)

question: What distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from routine chronic high blood pressure?

options.A: Acute, progressive damage to vital target organs
options.B: An isolated reading of 135/85 mmHg at rest
options.C: A mild headache lasting less than five minutes
options.D: The absence of any measurable pulse in the wrist

explanation: Emergency status is defined by active, dangerous damage to organs like the brain, heart, or kidneys. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h7)

question: Why must blood pressure be lowered gradually during a hypertensive emergency?

options.A: Quick drops cause the heart to stop beating completely
options.B: Slow reductions prevent the patient from feeling any discomfort
options.C: Rapid drops can cause cerebral ischemia and inadequate organ perfusion
options.D: Intravenous pumps cannot physically deliver drugs at a fast speed

explanation: Dropping pressure too fast deprives the brain and other organs of vital blood flow, risking stroke or ischemia. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h7)
